segments.t: The session journal documents a terminal session as a readable timeline: every server output line and every command you type is written to a capture log, an AI periodically condenses the activity into short journal entries, and the result is rendered as a self-contained HTML page with connection details, color-coded excerpts, screenshots and your own notes. Journals are managed like saved chats — in their own manager window with search, editing and export.
Each journal is one self-contained directory under KTPH000 (configurable in KTPH001Settings KTPH003 Logging KTPH004 Session JournalKTPH002):
The curated journal document: metadata, AI summaries, markers, notes, screenshot references
The append-only capture log — timestamped server output and typed input lines with sequence ids
Rotated log parts; closed parts are zstd-compressed automatically, the journal never deletes history. Journals recorded by older versions keep their KTPH000 parts and remain fully readable
The generated timeline page, regenerated automatically after every change
Screenshots you attached during the session

The capture-log format is selectable in the journal manager's KTPH006OptionsKTPH007 dialog: KTPH008JSONKTPH009 (JSON Lines, the default), KTPH010XMLKTPH011 or KTPH012YAMLKTPH013. All formats carry the same fields, and every entry is exactly one line, so a crash never corrupts more than the last line. JSON is the default because log tooling reads it without needing a parser of its own — not because it saves space. Size barely separates the three: for ordinary output XML is about 9 bytes per entry smaller, for output full of KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002 JSON is roughly 10 % smaller (XML has to escape those, JSON does not), and once a finished part is compressed all three land within 2 % of each other. YAML is the largest, since it writes JSON mappings with a KTPH003 prefix. The active log part stays uncompressed for live reads; rotation (default 25 MB per part) and session end compress finished parts to KTPH004 (zstd — journals from older versions keep their KTPH005 parts and open exactly as before).

Two more things keep long, noisy sessions small and complete. Consecutive identical output lines (progress loops, KTPH000 repeats) are coalesced syslog-style: the first occurrence is written immediately, follow-ups are counted and stored as one entry with a repeat count. The viewer shows such a run compactly as KTPH001, while copying or exporting the log reproduces the original lines in full. And when server output arrives faster than the log can persist it, the capture applies backpressure instead of dropping lines — the terminal may briefly slow down under an extreme flood, but the journal stays complete.

Rotation is configurable per connection on the KTPH001JournalKTPH002 tab: KTPH003Maximum size per log part (MB)KTPH004 (default 25) and KTPH005Maximum rotated log partsKTPH006 (default 20). After the configured number of parts, output capture stops with a note in the journal; input, screenshots and notes continue. An enterprise policy can cap the part count via KTPH000.
Open KTPH000Connections KTPH002 Manage ConnectionsKTPH001 and edit a connection
On the KTPH000JournalKTPH001 tab, enable KTPH002Enable session journal for this connectionKTPH003

Optionally adjust KTPH000Capture typed input linesKTPH001, KTPH002Generate AI summariesKTPH003, the per-connection KTPH004Summary intervalKTPH005, and the rotation pair KTPH006Maximum size per log part (MB)KTPH007 and KTPH008Maximum rotated log partsKTPH009
Every future connection of this server then starts its journal automatically. The journal survives reconnects — one journal per tab lifetime, with a reconnect marker in the log.

Use KTPH003Tools KTPH015 Start/Stop Session JournalKTPH004 (KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010), the tab context menu (KTPH011Session Journal KTPH016 Start journalKTPH012) or the journal bar's KTPH013Start journalKTPH014 button. The existing scrollback is imported into the journal as seed entries first, so the timeline covers what already happened, then live capture attaches.

While a journal is available, a bar below the terminal shows its state (KTPH000Journal active since HH:MMKTPH001) and offers KTPH002Stop journalKTPH003, KTPH004ScreenshotKTPH005 and KTPH006NoteKTPH007:

KTPH003ScreenshotKTPH004 (KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010, also in the terminal's right-click menu) snapshots the terminal — in a split layout, the right-click menu captures exactly the pane under the cursor — and files it into the journal timeline.
KTPH000NoteKTPH001 opens the KTPH002note editorKTPH003 for a free-text remark that appears as its own timeline entry at the current position.

Notes are written in the same editor everywhere they are edited — the journal bar's KTPH000NoteKTPH001 button, the live panel's, the entry form in the KTPH002viewerKTPH003, and the KTPH004screenshot editorKTPH005:
The field holds KTPH000at least six linesKTPH001 and the dialog can be resized, so a note can be a paragraph instead of a single line.

KTPH002Links are clickable.KTPH003 Any KTPH000 or KTPH001 address in a note becomes a link on the journal page — click it and the address opens in your system browser, never inside the journal view. Only those two schemes ever become links, and only in text you wrote yourself: AI summaries and terminal excerpts stay literal.

KTPH004TranslateKTPH005 hands the note to the AI and replaces it with the translation in the language picked next to the button. The list offers the interface languages and any language korTTY has translations for, and it accepts a typed language it does not list. Your choice is remembered for the next note. The translation runs on the profile assigned to KTPH006Text and translation profileKTPH007 in the KTPH008AI managerKTPH009 — the same role the snippet editor's translation uses — falling back to your default profile when that role is unset. Internet access stays disabled for it, exactly as for the summaries; KTPH010KTPH000KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013 / KTPH014KTPH002KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH003KTPH017 brings the original back. Without a usable AI profile the button is disabled and says so.

A journal is bound to its tab, not to a single connection. When the connection ends while the journal is running — a KTPH000, a dropped network, or the server closing the session — the tab KTPH001stays openKTPH002 and a red decision bar appears instead of the tab closing silently:
KTPH000ReconnectKTPH001 re-establishes the connection and the journal simply continues, with a reconnect marker in the capture log. Work that resumes after a server reboot lands in the same journal.

KTPH000End journalKTPH001 stops the journal and writes its closing summary (and, if enabled, the AI title) exactly like the journal bar's stop button. The tab then shows the plain reconnect bar, so reconnecting is still possible — with journaling enabled for the connection, that new session starts a fresh journal.

Closing the tab instead also ends the journal with its closing summary. Without a running journal the behavior is unchanged: a cleanly ended connection closes the tab, an error keeps it open with the reconnect bar (double-click to reconnect).

KTPH003View KTPH017 Live JournalKTPH004 (or KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010) docks the running journal's KTPH011full journal pageKTPH012 — the same page the KTPH013viewerKTPH014 shows — to the KTPH015left or rightKTPH016 of the terminal, kept up to date in real time. Selecting the checked side in the menu hides the panel again; the divider next to it adjusts the width, and side and width are remembered across restarts.
Two things update live while the session runs:

KTPH000The live logKTPH001 — the KTPH002Live LogKTPH003 button in the panel header opens the page's log panel in follow mode, streaming the capture log as it is written: command output, the commands you typed, notes and screenshot markers, each with a timestamp. It starts hidden; lines accumulate either way, so opening it later shows everything. Scrolling up pauses following, scrolling back to the bottom resumes it, the ✕ in its corner hides it again (the button stays in sync), and dragging its top edge adjusts the height — which is remembered. The view keeps the newest 5000 lines; everything stays in the capture log and in the entry cards' log excerpts.

KTPH000The timelineKTPH001 — new cards (AI summaries, notes, screenshots) and edits appear moments after they happen, without losing your scroll position. A KTPH002terminal AI-agentKTPH003 run adds its own KTPH004AI agentKTPH005 card the moment it finishes: your prompt as the title, the agent's final answer as the body, and a meta line with the model, the run duration and the reported token count. Long answers collapse to a preview — click the text (or KTPH006Show full answerKTPH007) to expand. Agent work is part of the journal record even though the summarizer treats the agent's inline terminal text as noise.

Because it is the real journal page, everything the viewer's page offers works right here: click an entry card to see its log excerpt, search the journal, jump between marked entries, and KTPH000right-clickKTPH001 a screenshot to open the KTPH002annotation editorKTPH003 (pen, box, unreadable, text and a note) or copy it — the edited picture appears in the panel as soon as you save. Right-clicking an entry offers the same marker picker as the viewer. The cards adapt to the panel width, so the text stays readable however narrow or wide you drag it.

The KTPH007◷KTPH008 button in the page header opens a time field: type a time and the timeline scrolls to the entry closest to it and highlights it briefly. The input is lenient — KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002 and KTPH003 all mean the same, and a date can be prefixed (KTPH004, KTPH005 or KTPH006). Without a date the time is matched against each entry's own day, so a session running past midnight jumps to the nearest occurrence rather than always the first day.

The panel's header adds the instant controls: KTPH000NoteKTPH001 and KTPH002ScreenshotKTPH003 act on the shown journal exactly like the KTPH004journal barKTPH005 — a note you add appears in both the timeline and the live log — KTPH006Live LogKTPH007 shows or hides the log view, and KTPH008Open ViewerKTPH009 opens the full viewer window for editing, search KTPH014 replace and exports. The KTPH010⋯KTPH011 menu switches the page between light and dark, refreshes it, and opens the page KTPH012appearanceKTPH013 settings.

The panel follows your tabs with a memory: it shows the journal of the current tab, and when you switch tabs it only switches along KTPH000if the newly selected tab also has a running journalKTPH001 — otherwise it keeps showing the journal it already displays. When the shown journal is stopped or its tab is closed, the page stays visible with a KTPH002Journal stoppedKTPH003 / KTPH004Tab closedKTPH005 badge until you select another tab with a live journal.
Everything shown has already passed KTPH000password protectionKTPH001 — suppressed input and redacted secrets never reach the panel.

While the journal runs, the AI summarizer periodically reads the newest capture-log lines and appends a compact journal entry (title, summary and a suggested marker: info, important or error). Defaults and limits:
KTPH000Settings KTPH002 Logging KTPH003 Session JournalKTPH001 (global) or per connection
Max. terminal lines per AI evaluation
Journal manager KTPH000OptionsKTPH001, visible when max lines is 0
Journal manager KTPH000OptionsKTPH001 or KTPH002Settings KTPH004 Logging KTPH005 Session JournalKTPH003
Analyze screenshots with AI (description and tags)

Summaries use your KTPH000default AI profileKTPH001 unless you pick a dedicated journal profile. That choice is available in three equivalent places: the journal manager's KTPH002OptionsKTPH003 dialog, KTPH004Settings KTPH008 Logging KTPH009 Session JournalKTPH005, and KTPH006AI KTPH010 AI Manager KTPH011 Local AIKTPH007 next to the Text and Coding roles. The Text/Coding role profiles themselves are deliberately not used for the journal.

Setting KTPH000max lines to 0KTPH001 switches to context filling: the summarizer packs as many of the newest lines as fit into the configured token budget. With KTPH002chunkingKTPH003 enabled the whole backlog is processed instead of only the newest window — consecutive windows of the configured size, one AI prompt each.
Chunking can take very long on large sessions and is not recommended for everyday use — it is intended for power users with capable hardware and a powerful LLM.

When the session ends, the summarizer writes a closing KTPH000session summaryKTPH001 entry (what was accomplished, which errors occurred) and extracts up to twelve verbatim KTPH002keywordsKTPH003 — hostnames, script and file names, error classes — into the journal metadata, where the manager's filter, keyword chips and KTPH004AI searchKTPH005 pick them up. Optionally — KTPH006Let the AI title the journal when the session endsKTPH007 in the Options dialog — a final AI call names the journal, unless you renamed it manually.

The journal works without AI: if no AI profile is available, AI features are disabled, or summaries are switched off, the timeline records raw activity entries instead. AI summary prompts never use internet-access tools; the terminal excerpt goes only to the configured AI profile.

When the journal's AI profile accepts images, screenshots are analyzed as well: the model writes a short KTPH000descriptionKTPH001 (one to three sentences) and a handful of lowercase KTPH002tagsKTPH003, shown to the right of the thumbnail on the journal page. Tags are clickable chips — clicking one starts a KTPH004journal searchKTPH005 for that tag — and both texts are found by the manager's KTPH006Search contentsKTPH007 scan, rewritten by KTPH008search and replaceKTPH009 and the automatic redaction rules, and included in the Markdown and PDF exports. Like the summaries, the analysis answers in the language the journal was created under.

KTPH000Analyze screenshots with AI (description and tags)KTPH001 in the journal manager's KTPH002OptionsKTPH003 dialog controls the automatic analysis on capture (on by default). It runs only when AI summaries are enabled for the connection and the profile can take images; otherwise the screenshot is simply filed unanalyzed.

KTPH001Analyze screenshot with AIKTPH002 in the right-click menu of a screenshot analyzes one picture on demand — the way to analyze screenshots in journals recorded earlier, to retry a failed run, or to re-run the analysis after making something unreadable in the KTPH003annotation editorKTPH004. The analysis always reads the annotated picture, never the untouched KTPH000 capture.

Whether a profile can take images is a per-profile property: KTPH000Image input (vision)KTPH001 in the KTPH002AI settingsKTPH003 defaults to KTPH004AutoKTPH005 — for a local LM Studio endpoint korTTY reads the answer from the model metadata (during the same refresh that discovers the reasoning options), for cloud endpoints it recognizes the common vision-capable model names — and can be overridden with KTPH006EnabledKTPH007/KTPH008DisabledKTPH009 for models the detection misjudges.

The automatic analysis sends the screenshot at capture time — before you had a chance to make anything unreadable. The picture goes only to the configured AI profile and never through internet-access tools, but for sessions whose screen content must not leave the machine, switch the option off or have your administrator forbid the analysis via KTPH000enterprise policyKTPH001 — the policy mandate also disables the manual run.
Asking the AI about a journalKTPH000

KTPH000AI QKTPH004AKTPH001 in the viewer's toolbar opens a chat panel next to the journal page. Ask anything about this session — KTPH002"Were screenshots taken that show errors from result_complex.pl?"KTPH003 — and the AI answers from what the journal already collected while the session ran: the AI summaries, screenshot descriptions and tags, and your notes. The raw capture log is never sent to the model.

When a question needs hard evidence from the log — exact error lines, whether a script really failed, how often something occurred — the model names a few literal search strings, korTTY's own streaming search scans the capture log for them, and only the match counts plus a handful of sample lines go back to the model for the final answer. The panel shows both next to the answer:
KTPH000SourcesKTPH001 — the journal entries the answer cites; clicking one scrolls the timeline to that entry.
KTPH000Log evidenceKTPH001 — per search string the exact number of matching log lines, with clickable samples that open the log panel scrolled to the very line.

Follow-up questions continue the conversation (the panel keeps the recent exchanges as context); KTPH000New conversationKTPH001 starts over. KTPH002Save as noteKTPH003 appends a question-and-answer pair to the journal timeline as an entry, so a finding becomes part of the record.

If no AI profile is reachable or the request fails, the panel degrades instead of erroring out: it extracts the identifiers from your question, runs the internal text search, and shows the matching entries and log lines with a notice that no model was involved. The QKTPH003A never uses internet-access tools, and administrators can forbid it entirely (KTPH000 under KTPH001enterprise policyKTPH002).
Typed input is captured only as complete submitted lines, and several layers keep passwords out of the journal:

When the server output ends in a password prompt (KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, and localized variants), the next submitted input line is suppressed and logged as a redacted placeholder — the typed text is never buffered or written.
The connection's own stored password is additionally replaced by KTPH000 wherever it would appear in captured text.
KTPH000Capture typed input linesKTPH001 can be disabled per connection entirely; commands then only appear as the server's echo in the output stream.

The prompt detection is a heuristic — a remote terminal cannot reliably know when the server disabled echo. Exotic or full-screen password prompts may not be recognized, and secrets pasted into visible commands (other than the connection's own credentials) are captured like any other text. Treat journals of sensitive sessions accordingly.

If something slipped through anyway, the viewer's KTPH000search and replaceKTPH001 removes it from the entries and the capture log after the fact. Administrators can also have korTTY redact patterns automatically — see KTPH002Enterprise policyKTPH003 below.
KTPH000 is fully self-contained (no external resources) and works in the built-in viewer, in any browser, and inside the exported bundle:

A sticky header shows who was connected to which server, start time, duration, and counts for entries, commands, errors and screenshots, plus the journal description. Live journals show a KTPH000liveKTPH001 badge. The line below the title only carries what the title does not already say, so a journal named after its endpoint states the connection once instead of three times.

The timeline groups entries by day; each entry carries its time, a marker dot and badge in the colour you gave that marker, the AI title and summary, and color-coded input (green) and output (blue) excerpts.

Clicking an entry slides a log panel in from the bottom with the exact capture-log range behind that entry. The panel has its own scrollbar, a search field with a match counter and ▲/▼ navigation (KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 / KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH002KTPH009 also cycle matches, KTPH010KTPH003KTPH011 closes), and colors input and output lines differently.

Screenshot entries show thumbnails; clicking one opens a full-size lightbox. If the KTPH000AI screenshot analysisKTPH001 ran, its description and tag chips sit to the right of the picture, and a chip click searches the journal for that tag.
The page renders dark by default, follows the system light/dark preference and has its own theme toggle.

Rules are checked from top to bottom and the first match wins — use ▲/▼ to order them. They look at the entry's title, summary, note and the input/output excerpts, never at the raw capture log, and they run after the redaction rules, so a redacted secret can never trigger one.

The text to find and what to put in its place (KTPH000 by default)
Treats the search text as a regex; KTPH000 in the replacement inserts a captured group

On by default. Off changes only the journal entries and leaves the raw log untouched
A dry run over the real journal: reports how many entry fields and log lines KTPH000wouldKTPH001 change, without writing anything

Replacing covers every entry title, AI summary, note and excerpt, and — unless you turned it off — every capture-log part including the compressed ones. The file header and every untouched line are preserved exactly, so the log keeps its structure.

The KTPH000ExportKTPH001 menu in the manager and the viewer offers three formats:
The simple journal: header with connection details and statistics, day-grouped entries with marker badges, input/output excerpts, notes — and, if selected, downscaled embedded screenshots
The same simple journal as a KTPH000 file; screenshots are copied into a sibling KTPH001 folder
A zip archive of the whole journal — KTPH000, KTPH001, the decompressed capture logs and all screenshots — laid out so the page works immediately after unzipping

Exporting only part of a journalKTPH000
The export dialog can narrow down what actually goes into the document. Every filter is optional, and the footer keeps a live count of how many entries would be exported.

The times may be approximate — that is the point:
The input is forgiving: KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003 and KTPH004 all work.

An entry summarizes everything since the previous one, so an entry written at 12:03 that covers 11:58 onwards still belongs to a window ending at 12:00. Without that, the entry on the boundary — usually the interesting one — would fall out of every window.

KTPH000Topic.KTPH001 A word or a sentence, matched against titles, summaries, notes and excerpts; KTPH002Regular expressionKTPH003 switches to regex matching. KTPH004Let the AI choose the entriesKTPH005 hands the topic and the entries to the AI instead, which finds KTPH006installing ApacheKTPH007 even where none of those words appear literally. Without a filter the HTML bundle stays the verbatim copy it always was. With one it is KTPH000rebuiltKTPH001:
KTPH000 holds only the exported entries, and the marker definitions travel with them.

The capture log is rewritten to the sequence ranges those entries reference, clipped to the requested time windows. This is not optional — a bundle is the artefact you hand to someone else, and twelve entries next to eight hours of terminal output would be exactly the leak the filter is meant to prevent.
Only the screenshots still referenced are copied, and KTPH000 is re-rendered so its deep links resolve.
The header counts are recalculated to match what the bundle shows.
Every filtered export — PDF, Markdown and bundle alike — carries an KTPH000ExcerptKTPH001 banner naming the range and the entry count, so nobody mistakes it for the complete session.

With more than one journal selected, the export writes a single zip archive that keeps each journal separate: one PDF or Markdown document per journal, or one folder per journal for the HTML bundle. Names are taken from the journal titles, with a numeric suffix if two titles collide.

Filters apply to every selected journal. A journal in which the filter matches nothing is skipped and reported afterwards, so one empty result cannot kill a ten-journal export; only if KTPH000everyKTPH001 journal comes out empty does the export refuse — before writing a file.

Journals contain full terminal transcripts, so an unprotected archive is a deliberate choice.
The password is not stored anywhere. korTTY cannot recover an encrypted archive if you lose it.

By default every exported document carries a footer stating that it was created with korTTY, with a link to the project repository — at the bottom of each PDF page, at the end of the Markdown file, and in the footer of the journal page inside the HTML bundle.
